14                THE SECRETARY:   Legislative 

15   Resolution Number 352, by Senator Golden,  

16   commemorating the Asian-American community's 

17   celebration of the Lunar New Year, 4713, the 

18   Year of the Ram, on February 19, 2015.

19                ACTING PRESIDENT VALESKY:   Senator 

20   Golden on the resolution.

21                SENATOR GOLDEN:   Thank you, 

22   Mr. President.  

23                Next Thursday, February 19th, 

24   Asian-Americans across our state will gather to 

25   celebrate the year 4713 in the Lunar New Year 


                                                                385

 1   calendar.  

 2                For those who are not from New York 

 3   City, when immigrants moved to the New York City 

 4   neighborhoods, they were built all up and around 

 5   and shared a heritage that in many cases persists 

 6   to this day.  There is no denying the impact that 

 7   the Asian-Americans have had on New York City.  

 8   One of the most popular tourist destinations in 

 9   all of New York City is Manhattan's Chinatown.  

10                And the Asian population has grown, 

11   not just in New York City but throughout our 

12   state and throughout our nation.  One-sixth of 

13   all students in New York City public schools are 

14   Asian-Americans.  

15                The tradition tells us that the 

16   Jade Emperor once invited all the animals of the 

17   world to visit with him.  Those animals that 

18   heeded the invitation were honored by having 

19   years named after them.  And February 19th marks 

20   the beginning of the Year of the Ram.  

21                Individuals born during the Year of 

22   the Ram are said to be embody certain 

23   characteristics that can be connected to their 

24   birth year.  They are known for their shyness, 

25   their generosity, their kindness of nature and 


                                                                386

 1   their empathy for others, the sorts of qualities 

 2   that should be celebrated all year long.  

 3                The ram is the eighth animal in the 

 4   Chinese zodiac, which places them and those born 

 5   in that Year of the Ram in a favorable position 

 6   in China, because in China the number 8 

 7   represents peace and prosperity.

 8                This year the Chinese community has 

 9   much to celebrate, as my legislation has passed 

10   last year allowing schools to close -- working 

11   here with Senator Squadron and others here in 

12   this great legislative body -- to close in 

13   observance of the Lunar New Year.  And if the 

14   school's governing authority sees fit, they can 

15   and will close.  And that was signed into law by 

16   Governor Cuomo in December.

17                And I cannot wait to celebrate this 

18   Lunar New Year with the Asian-Americans I 

19   represent in my district, because for Lunar 

20   New Year we do a great celebration on March 1st 

21   and we have thousands of people come out and 

22   celebrate with us.

23                The Lunar New Year is one of the 

24   greatest cultural holidays.  And it has become a 

25   great holiday in New York State because of the 


                                                                387

 1   impact on the community it has had on New York 

 2   State, and it's prosperous and it has grown in 

 3   many, many numbers over the years.  

 4                And I'm proud to represent such a 

 5   large Asian-American population, and I'd like to 

 6   wish all who celebrate a peaceful and prosperous 

 7   Year of the Ram.

 8                Thank you, Mr. President.

 9                ACTING PRESIDENT VALESKY:   Thank 

10   you, Senator Golden.

11                Senator Squadron on the resolution.

12                SENATOR SQUADRON:   Thank you, 

13   Mr. President.  

14                And I too rise to acknowledge the 

15   upcoming Lunar New Year festivities and 

16   celebration, and the upcoming Year of the Ram.  I 

17   thank Senator Golden for his detailed description 

18   of -- what we sometimes call, in Chinese culture, 

19   Talmudic description -- of the Year of the Ram 

20   and its significance.

21                It's an important year, as each of 

22   the years of the lunar calendar is.  But even 

23   more, it's a really important festival and 

24   acknowledgment for the entire state of our 

25   growing Asian-American community, not just in my 


                                                                388

 1   district in Chinatown -- which is really the 

 2   heart and the history of the cultural life of the 

 3   Chinese experience in America, certainly on the 

 4   East Coast -- but across New York City from 

 5   Brooklyn to Queens and across our entire state 

 6   and nation.

 7                The significance and importance of 

 8   our Asian-American community is so important.  

 9   And Lunar New Year is a time of the year when we 

10   can acknowledge that, when we can enjoy as an 

11   entire state community the vibrance, the 

12   importance, the cultural celebration that it 

13   brings.  

14                It's particularly important, 

15   actually, just for the small businesses and the 

16   residents who still live in the various 

17   Chinese-American communities across the city.  If 

18   you are looking for an experience that will make 

19   you fall in love with New York City and New York 

20   State again, join one of the Lunar New Year 

21   parades, whether in Sunset Park or in Chinatown 

22   or in Flushing.  Come down and enjoy the 

23   restaurants, the absolutely extraordinary 

24   cuisine, the stores, and help support the economy 

25   at the same time that we are respecting and 


                                                                389

 1   acknowledging such an important cultural 

 2   heritage.

 3                And as Senator Golden referenced, 

 4   last year, working with Senator Golden, 

 5   Senator Stavisky and others, we were able to push 

 6   forward the idea that parents should not have to 

 7   be forced between the most important cultural 

 8   celebration of their year and their family's year 

 9   and missing a day of school by having a Lunar 

10   New Year school holiday.  And this year, luckily, 

11   the school calendar for the Year of the Ram 

12   cooperated.  We will have a school holiday.  And 

13   I am confident that working together we will have 

14   that school holiday for many years to come.

15                So entering this month of festivity, 

16   parades, banquets, more better food than you 

17   could ever imagine eating, I invite all of my 

18   colleagues from anywhere in the state to join us 

19   in Chinatown for the parade, for any of these 

20   banquets.  I promise you that you will really 

21   again remember why we are so proud to be 

22   New Yorkers, why it is that the world comes to 

23   New York and flourishes and makes New York that 

24   much stronger.  

25                Happy Year of the Ram to the entire 


                                                                390

 1   New York State community.  

 2                Thank you, Mr. President.

17                THE SECRETARY:   Legislative 

18   Resolution Number 443, by Senator 

19   Stewart-Cousins, memorializing Governor Andrew M. 

20   Cuomo to proclaim February 2015 as Black History 

21   Month in the State of New York.  

22                "WHEREAS, Black History Month, 

23   previously known as Negro History Week, was 

24   founded by Dr. Carter G. Woodson, and was first 

25   celebrated on February 1, 1926; since 1976, it 


                                                                391

 1   has become a nationally recognized month-long 

 2   celebration, held each year during the month of  

 3   February to acknowledge and pay tribute to  

 4   African-Americans neglected by both society and 

 5   the history books; and 

 6                "WHEREAS, The month of February 

 7   observes the rich and diverse heritage of our 

 8   great state and nation; and 

 9                "WHEREAS, Black History Month seeks 

10   to emphasize Black History is American History; 

11   and 

12                "WHEREAS, Black History Month is a 

13   time to reflect on the struggles and victories of 

14   African-Americans throughout our country's 

15   history and to recognize their numerous valuable 

16   contributions to the protection of our democratic 

17   society in war and in peace; and 

18                "WHEREAS, Some African-American 

19   pioneers whose many accomplishments, all of which 

20   took place during the month of February, went  

21   unnoticed, as well as numerous symbolic events in  

22   February that deserve to be memorialized include: 

23   John Sweat Rock, a noted Boston lawyer who  

24   became the first African-American admitted to 

25   argue before the U.S. Supreme Court on 


                                                                392

 1   February 1, 1865, and the first African-American 

 2   to be received on the floor of the U.S. House of 

 3   Representatives; Jonathan Jasper Wright, the 

 4   first  African-American to hold a major judicial 

 5   position, who was elected to the South Carolina 

 6   Supreme Court on February 1, 1870; President 

 7   Abraham Lincoln submits the proposed Thirteenth 

 8   Amendment to the U.S. Constitution, abolishing 

 9   slavery, to the states for ratification on 

10   February 1, 1865; civil rights protester Jimmie 

11   Lee Jackson dies from wounds inflicted during a 

12   protest on February 26, 1965, leading to the 

13   historic Selma, Alabama, civil rights 

14   demonstrations, including Bloody Sunday, in which 

15   600 demonstrators, including  Martin Luther King, 

16   Jr., were attacked by police; Autherine J. Lucy 

17   became the first African-American student to 

18   attend the University of Alabama on February 3, 

19   1956, but was expelled three days later 'for her 

20   own safety' in response to threats from a mob; in 

21   1992, Autherine Lucy Foster graduated from the 

22   university with a master's degree in education, 

23   the same day her daughter, Grazia Foster,  

24   graduated with a bachelor's degree in corporate  

25   finance; the Negro Baseball League was founded on 


                                                                393

 1   February 3, 1920; Jack Johnson, the first 

 2   African-American World Heavyweight Boxing 

 3   Champion, won his first title on February 3, 

 4   1903; and Reginald F. Lewis, born on December 7, 

 5   1942, in Baltimore, Maryland, received his law 

 6   degree from Harvard Law School in 1968, and was a 

 7   partner in Murphy, Thorpes & Lewis, the first 

 8   black law firm on Wall Street, and in 1989, he 

 9   became president and CEO of TLC Beatrice 

10   International Food Company, the largest 

11   black-owned business in the United States; and 

12                "WHEREAS, In recognition of the vast 

13   contributions of African-Americans, a joyful 

14   month-long celebration is held across New York 

15   State and across the United States with many 

16   commemorative events to honor and display the 

17   cultural heritage of African-Americans; and 

18                "WHEREAS, This Legislative Body 

19   commends the African-American community for 

20   preserving, for future generations, its 

21   centuries-old traditions that benefit us all and 

22   add to the color and beauty of the tapestry which 

23   is our American society; now, therefore, be it 

24                "RESOLVED, That this Legislative 

25   Body pause in its deliberations to memorialize  


                                                                394

 1   Governor Andrew M. Cuomo to proclaim February 

 2   2015 as Black History Month in the State of 

 3   New York; and be it further 

 4                "RESOLVED, That copies of this 

 5   resolution, suitably engrossed, be transmitted  

 6   to the Honorable Andrew M. Cuomo, Governor of the 

 7   State of New York, and to the events 

 8   commemorating Black History Month throughout 

 9   New York State."

10                ACTING PRESIDENT VALESKY:   Senator 

11   Stewart-Cousins on the resolution.

12                SENATOR STEWART-COUSINS:   Thank 

13   you, Mr. President.

14                I rise again to speak about Black 

15   History Month.  It's something that we do 

16   annually, and it's an opportunity that I like to 

17   take to again tell people of the rich history and 

18   the contributions of African-Americans not only 

19   to our state but to our country and to the world.

20                Last month we celebrated Dr. Martin 

21   Luther King, Jr.'s birthday, and we all know and 

22   remember what Dr. King has meant to, again, our 

23   community as well as humanity.  This month there 

24   are so many different people to talk about, and 

25   many of them were named in the resolution.  But I 


                                                                395

 1   wanted to spend a moment to remember two unsung 

 2   heroes in my own community.  

 3                I unfortunately had to attend two 

 4   funerals of black pioneers in the Westchester 

 5   area who made a difference.  One was Rita 

 6   Gross-Nelson.  

 7                Rita Gross-Nelson was the first 

 8   African-American woman police officer in the 

 9   City of Yonkers.  In a city that has gone through 

10   many ups and downs and trials and tribulations 

11   and desegregation cases, Rita Gross-Nelson stood 

12   tall and proud.  She understood what community 

13   policing meant.  There was never anyone in Rita's 

14   path that she wouldn't want to help, serve and 

15   protect.

16                Rita was also the first black female 

17   to become a detective in the City of Yonkers, and 

18   she led the way and opened doors for many others 

19   to come behind her.  And to have an exemplary 

20   example of professionalism, policing compassion, 

21   and, again, trailblazing attitudes during her 

22   years of service.

23                The other great pioneer that we 

24   lost, at age 95, was the great Dorothy Orr.  

25                Dorothy Orr was an associate 


                                                                396

 1   professor at Fordham University.  She was a 

 2   commissioner of the New York State Division of 

 3   Human Rights.  But Dorothy too was a pathfinder 

 4   and a trailblazer.  She was the very first vice 

 5   president of a national insurance company who 

 6   happened to be African-American and female.  

 7                She opened corporations' doors to 

 8   the understanding that in order to really broaden 

 9   their influence, broaden their profit margin, and 

10   broaden their credibility, they needed to have 

11   all voices at the table.  And Dorothy Orr opened 

12   doors and let those other voices in.

13                So in this resolution I wanted to 

14   make sure that we understood that there are 

15   heroes that change our lives, obviously 

16   nationally noted and then right in our 

17   communities and, yes, right here in our 

18   Legislature.

19                I had an opportunity to have lunch 

20   with the executive director of a very well known 

21   agency in New York City.  His name was Mr. David 

22   Jones.  He talked about his father, who was the 

23   second black Assemblyman in New York State's 

24   Legislature, the Judge Thomas Jones.

25                Thomas Jones served in the Assembly 


                                                                397

 1   in 1963 and 1964 before he became a judge.  And I 

 2   asked David why he knew so much about the 

 3   legislative work that we did, and he said that it 

 4   was because his father recruited him to put the 

 5   bills on the desks in the Assembly because, when 

 6   his dad was an Assemblyman in 1963, the pages 

 7   would not put the bills on his desk as a black 

 8   man.  Black history.  

 9                And today we are here celebrating 

10   the first African-American Assembly speaker, 

11   Carl Heastie.

12                So the reality is there have been 

13   many, many, many, many roads traveled, many doors 

14   opened.  We are excited about the opportunity 

15   that the speakership of Carl Heastie brings.  We 

16   are excited that between 1963 and 2015 not only 

17   do we all get the proper information on our 

18   desks, but we are rising to the highest levels of 

19   leadership.

20                It is black history, it is American 

21   history, and it is certainly history that when we 

22   keep our eye on the prize, not only do black 

23   people rise but humanity rises.  

24                So thank you very much, appreciate 

25   it.


                                                                398

 1                ACTING PRESIDENT VALESKY:   Thank 

 2   you, Senator Stewart-Cousins.

 3                Senator Larkin on the resolution.

 4                SENATOR LARKIN:   Thank you very 

 5   much, Mr. President.

 6                I'm very -- excuse me.  You know, 

 7   this is the very issue that I think we ought to 

 8   sit down -- I wish there was more people in the 

 9   chamber.  

10                But think about it.  My history with 

11   African-American soldiers goes back to OCS, which 

12   is called Officer's Candidate School.  Eric Hill, 

13   from Kansas, a state policeman, sat across -- his 

14   bed was across from mine.  When we went to 

15   Benning in '49, they said:  "You two can have 

16   mess here, and you can go down to the enlisted 

17   men mess."  Well, Mike Krushevksi and I tore up 

18   our officers club card and walked out and went to 

19   the enlisted men's mess.  

20                Hill was one of the first killed in 

21   our class in Korea.  

22                And when you think about it, the 

23   blood that spatters, not only then but years 

24   before and now, we stop arguing about little 

25   petty things and start to think about what the 


                                                                399

 1   nation does when we honor.  We're talking about 

 2   Black History Month.  

 3                How many of our kids today -- I 

 4   asked a whole bunch of them in the last two 

 5   weeks:  "What do you know about March of 1965?"  

 6   "I don't know, I wasn't born."  "Did you go home 

 7   and ask your parents?"  "They don't know."

 8                March of 1965, the March from Selma 

 9   to Montgomery.  I don't know where Bill -- Bill 

10   Perkins, one of his constituents and I were part 

11   of the march.  Not marchers, he was a marshal and 

12   I was an Army project officer.

13                And when you saw the people on the 

14   sideline ready to slap somebody or do something, 

15   all that it did was encourage people to march.  

16                Now, people will tell you there were 

17   600, there were 900.  There were 2500 the very 

18   first day.  Black, white, pink, green, all 

19   marching for one thing, to make it so that these 

20   individuals, American citizens, were treated like 

21   everybody else.

22                George Wallace looked out the window 

23   the day we arrived to give him the orders to 

24   activate the Guard.  And he said, "I won't 

25   activate the Guard for those" -- you know what he 


                                                                400

 1   said.  But then that night, at 11 o'clock, I was 

 2   ordered to issue him another one that says, from 

 3   the President of the United States, we're 

 4   activating all of the Guard in Alabama.  

 5                And you notice the Guard coming in 

 6   from the rest of the nation -- the 101st, 

 7   2nd Armored, 11th Air Assault -- they weren't 

 8   just all white, they were black and white.  

 9                What happened?  The 26th of July, 

10   1948, President Truman said desegregate.  The 

11   problem is a lot of people were slow on the draw.  

12                But at Fort Benning, after we didn't 

13   get dinner that night, the next day I got called 

14   and somebody said, "Boy, are you going to get 

15   your you-know-what kicked today."  And I went in, 

16   and there was a major general that I served with 

17   when he was a colonel and I was a lieutenant.  

18   And he said, quote, "At 5 o'clock tonight, every 

19   sign that indicates nondiversity will be taken 

20   down, and anybody who doesn't comply will answer 

21   to me."  

22                Now, you know in '49 I went to Japan 

23   and there was an exchange of commanders.  I was 

24   the youngest lieutenant.  And somebody said to 

25   me, "Who did you make mad?  You got this black 


                                                                401

 1   company."  I said, "You're wrong.  I got the 

 2   212th."  He said "Larkin's is the worst company."  

 3   I said "Mark my word."  

 4                And we worked together, and we 

 5   treated people alike.  We made sure that 

 6   education was an opportunity, not just for 

 7   somebody.  The average education in my company at 

 8   that time, with the exception of a few, was 6th 

 9   grade.  Today you couldn't even get in the Army 

10   with a 6th-grade education.

11                But everybody worked together as a 

12   team.  In April 1950, the 212th, the all-black 

13   company -- and I used to kid them that it's not 

14   all black, there's five of us white guys sticking 

15   around here someplace, and it was a big joke -- 

16   they were number one.  And when General 

17   Eichelberger said "Bring up your officers," I 

18   said "No.  You see all these ladies over there 

19   with the white hats?  They're the mothers of this 

20   outfit."  And they came up and got the award.

21                You know, every day we run against 

22   people -- or run into them, I mean, and we have 

23   differences.  I had it in my own family.  My 

24   daughter said, "I'm going to Africa, my husband 

25   and I are missionaries."  They just returned from 


                                                                402

 1   27 years.  We have five grandchildren out of 

 2   there.  They speak French, Portuguese, a little 

 3   German and, proudly, English.  They're proud.  

 4   I'm proud of them.  

 5                But you know, think about what we 

 6   do.  Newburgh Police Department came to me over 

 7   the weekend and said, "We don't have any black 

 8   officers."  I said "Why don't we?"  "Because 

 9   nobody passed the test."

10                So that's ours, as elected 

11   officials.  What are we doing to help eliminate 

12   this problem?  We will start tomorrow talking to 

13   the state and a few others, and we're going to 

14   put a program on to teach them how to take the 

15   test, how to be an officer.

16                I want to tell you something.  Black 

17   history, we really should change it to say 

18   American history, because it's our history.  It's 

19   not anybody else's, it's all of ours.  

20                How you handle these issues, I don't 

21   know -- I'm 87 -- how many more I'll be here to 

22   see.  But I want to tell you, my pride in those I 

23   served with and those that I know are still 

24   serving are part of history we should never 

25   forget.
